scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `adaptyv` skill is a documentation-only reference package for the Adaptyv Bio Foundry REST API and Python SDK. It contains no executable scripts — only SKILL.md and a single internal reference file (`references/api-endpoints.md`) that is a faithful, benign API endpoint catalog. No prompt injection, instruction overrides, concealment directives, obfuscation, encoded payloads, credential exfiltration, command injection, or unauthorized network egress were detected. All URLs and domains are first-party vendor endpoints consistent with the stated purpose, and the declared `allowed-tools` (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the documented install/export/curl operations. Secret handling guidance is actually good practice (env vars, no hardcoding, no committing). The only issues are minor hygiene concerns: an unpinned GitHub VCS dependency install, documented auto-accept-quote automation that could incur costs without human review, agent access to .env credential material, broad passive activation triggers, and three referenced files that do not exist in the package. Overall risk: LOW — the skill appears legitimate and non-malicious.

findings.title: Instructs reading API key from environment and local .env files
findings.description: The skill directs the agent to locate and load a `.env` file from the project root and to read `ADAPTYV_API_KEY` from the environment. This is standard, recommended secret-handling practice (it explicitly warns against hardcoding or committing tokens) and no exfiltration path exists, but it does involve the agent touching credential material, which warrants awareness.
findings.snippet: "always read the API key from the environment variable `ADAPTYV_API_KEY` or from a `.env` file — never hardcode tokens. Check for a `.env` file in the project root first"
findings.remediation: Ensure the agent only passes the key to the documented Adaptyv API endpoint and never echoes, logs, or writes key values into files or chat output.

findings.title: Documented workflow bypasses human review for billable operations
findings.description: A documented 'Automated Pipeline' pattern sets `skip_draft: true` and `auto_accept_quote: true`, which bypasses the Draft review stage and auto-accepts a financial quote, generating a Stripe invoice without a human confirmation step. If the agent applies this pattern autonomously it could commit the user to real laboratory costs. This is a legitimate vendor API feature, not malicious, but it is an autonomy/financial-risk pattern.
findings.snippet:
"skip_draft": True,
"auto_accept_quote": True,
findings.remediation: Add an explicit instruction that the agent must obtain user confirmation before setting `auto_accept_quote` or `skip_draft`, since these create binding financial commitments.

findings.title: Broad activation triggers including code-import and domain detection
findings.description: The description specifies many activation triggers, including automatic triggering when code imports `adaptyv`, `adaptyv_sdk`, or `FoundryClient`, or references the vendor domain. These triggers are all tightly scoped to the vendor's own namespace and product terminology, so this is reasonable rather than keyword baiting, but it does slightly widen passive activation surface (the skill can activate from file content rather than explicit user request).
findings.snippet: "Also trigger when code imports `adaptyv`, `adaptyv_sdk`, or `FoundryClient`, or references `foundry-api-public.adaptyvbio.com`."
findings.remediation: No change strictly required; optionally narrow activation to explicit user intent rather than passive code-content matching.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installed directly from GitHub
findings.description: The skill instructs installation of `adaptyv-sdk` directly from a GitHub repository (`git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git`) without any version, tag, or commit pin. While the repository appears to be the vendor's official one and matches the documented domain, unpinned VCS installs mean whatever code is on the default branch at install time is executed, creating a supply-chain exposure if the repo or account is ever compromised.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install "git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git"
uv add "adaptyv-sdk @ git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git"
findings.remediation: Pin the dependency to a specific tag or commit hash (e.g., `git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git@v0.1.0` or `@<commit-sha>`), and prefer PyPI with hash verification once published.

findings.title: Referenced files declared but missing from package
findings.description: The skill references `adaptyv.py`, `templates/api-endpoints.md`, and `assets/api-endpoints.md`, none of which are present in the package. Only `references/api-endpoints.md` exists. Missing referenced files can lead to the agent searching for or fabricating substitutes, and could become a resolution hazard if files with those names later appear from untrusted sources.
findings.snippet: Referenced but not found: adaptyv.py, templates/api-endpoints.md, assets/api-endpoints.md
findings.remediation: Remove references to non-existent files or bundle them in the package; keep documentation references limited to files actually shipped with the skill.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The admet-prediction skill is a documentation-heavy cheminformatics helper and appears benign. Both bundled Python scripts (admet_batch.py, admet_report.py) use only the standard library (argparse, csv, json, pathlib, sys): they read a user-specified SMILES/CSV file, chunk it, write CSV chunks plus a manifest.json into a user-specified output directory, and parse ADMET-AI prediction CSVs to emit TSV/CSV/JSON to stdout. There is no networking, no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no dynamic imports, no environment-variable or credential access, no base64/obfuscated payloads, and no file access outside explicitly user-supplied paths. Printed `admet_predict ...` command lines are emitted as text for the user to review, not executed. The SKILL.md body and the three bundled reference files contain no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or instructions to fetch and trust external content; the only external URLs are informational citations (GitHub project, public web predictor) and the docs explicitly warn against sending proprietary structures to the public web service. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the observed behavior of reading inputs and writing chunk/manifest files. Several referenced paths under templates/ and assets/ are not found, but the canonical references/ copies exist, so this is a path-resolution artifact rather than a security issue. Only two low-severity, informational observations were recorded.

findings.title: Trigger-keyword list in skill description
findings.description: The YAML description ends with an explicit activation-keyword list ('Also trigger on ADMET-AI, admet_ai, Chemprop-RDKit, hERG liability, CYP3A4 inhibition, Caco-2, bioavailability prediction, or developability triage'). This is a mild discovery-optimization pattern. All listed terms are narrowly scoped to the skill's actual cheminformatics/ADMET domain, and no brand impersonation, priority manipulation, or over-broad ('can do anything') claims are present, so the risk is informational only.
findings.snippet: Also trigger on ADMET-AI, admet_ai, Chemprop-RDKit, hERG liability, CYP3A4 inhibition, Caco-2, bioavailability prediction, or developability triage.
findings.remediation: Optional: trim the explicit trigger-keyword enumeration to a plain functional description to minimize unintended skill activation.

findings.title: Unpinned third-party package installation instruction
findings.description: Documentation instructs the user to run `pip install admet-ai` without a pinned version, which pulls chemprop, RDKit, and PyTorch and downloads model weights from the network on first use. findings.title: Unbounded paging walk with retry backoff can consume significant time and network resources

Combined with up to 4 retries per request and sleeps of up to 30 seconds, a broad query can produce long-running, request-heavy execution. Defaults are bounded (--limit 50/200) and the documentation explicitly warns about cost, so this is a mild efficiency/availability consideration rather than an abuse pattern.

request_params["pageSize"] = min(page_size, MAX_PAGE_SIZE)
while True: ... token = document.get("nextPageToken")
findings.remediation: Enforce a hard upper bound on total pages/records fetched per invocation and cap cumulative retry sleep time.

findings.description: The HTTP base URL is read from the CTGOV_API_URL environment variable and can also be overridden with --base-url. _build_url() additionally short-circuits and returns any path that already begins with http:// or https://. ...
if path.startswith("http://") or path.startswith("https://"):
    return path
findings.remediation: Restrict the override to an allow-list of trusted hosts (or require https and reject non-clinicaltrials.gov hosts unless explicitly confirmed), and drop the absolute-URL passthrough in _build_url.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The ncats-arax skill is a documentation-only package (no scripts were delivered) that describes a tightly constrained client for the public NCATS Translator ARAX biomedical knowledge-graph API. No prompt injection, instruction-override, concealment, jailbreak, or role-redefinition language was found in SKILL.md or either reference file. There are no hardcoded credentials, no obfuscated or encoded payloads, no eval/exec/os.system patterns, no credential-path reads (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), no environment-variable harvesting, no dependency installation, and no filesystem traversal or over-collection. The manifest description is narrow, accurately scoped, and explicitly enumerates non-uses (no inference, ranking, open-ended pathfinding, clinical guidance, or sensitive queries), so there is no capability inflation or keyword baiting. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Bash) are consistent with the described behavior of reading bundled reference files and invoking a local Python CLI. Security posture is notably defensive: strict CURIE/Biolink/infores regex validation before interpolation into ARAXi actions, a fixed non-extensible operation set, an explicit list of excluded escape hatches (no raw JSON submission, workflow, operations, overlay, MCP, daemon, or server surfaces), a 25 MiB bounded response read, HTTPS-only base URLs with rejection of loopback/private/link-local addresses and cross-origin or protocol-downgrade redirects, no automatic retry of POST /query, a constant submitter string that excludes user-identifying data, 0600 artifact permissions with atomic writes, and mandatory explicit acknowledgment that queries are public. Only low-severity hygiene issues were identified: the referenced arax_client.py script is not bundled, outbound transmission of query content to a third party is inherent to the stated purpose, and a forward-dated verification claim appears in the documentation.

findings.title: Outbound network transmission of user query content to a third-party service
findings.description: The skill, by design, POSTs user-supplied biomedical identifiers and query parameters to the external endpoint https://arax.transltr.io/api/arax/v1.4 and performs GET requests against /openapi.json and /entity. This is the declared purpose of the skill and the endpoint is the legitimate public NCATS Translator ARAX service, so it is not covert exfiltration. The skill explicitly warns that query and caller metadata may be publicly visible, requires an `--acknowledge-public-query` flag, forbids embedding user/project names in the submitter or User-Agent, restricts base URLs to HTTPS without credentials, and rejects loopback/private/link-local targets and cross-origin or protocol-downgrade redirects. Noted for data-flow awareness only.
findings.snippet: **Endpoint:** `https://arax.transltr.io/api/arax/v1.4` - POST TRAPI, no key. ... Every normalization or graph request requires `--acknowledge-public-query`.
findings.remediation: No change required. Retain the explicit public-query acknowledgment, the constant submitter string, and the HTTPS/no-private-address URL policy; continue to prohibit automatic fallback to alternate ARA endpoints.

findings.title: Unverifiable future-dated provenance claim in documentation

findings.remediation: Replace the hard-coded verification date with an accurate last-tested date and rely on the runtime `preflight` version check as the authoritative compatibility signal.

No network calls, no subprocess/os.system, no eval/exec, no credential or environment access, no file writes outside stdout/stderr, no obfuscated or encoded payloads, and no package installation. The subject matter is dual-use in a general sense (therapeutic oligonucleotide design) but the content is standard, publicly documented pharmacology with explicit safety framing. findings.title: Unbounded O(n*m) substring scan over user-supplied transcriptome FASTA
findings.description: offtarget_scan.py's `contig` command runs `longest_common_substring` for every candidate against every record of a user-supplied FASTA, and `read_fasta` loads the entire file into memory. With a full transcriptome FASTA (hundreds of MB) and many candidates this can consume large amounts of CPU and RAM. There is no record-count, size, or runtime limit. This is a performance/robustness issue rather than an intentional denial-of-service, and the input is supplied by the user themselves.

for transcript_name, sequence in transcripts.items():

findings.remediation: Document expected FASTA sizes, stream records instead of loading all into memory, and add optional caps on the number of records/candidates processed.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The open-targets skill is a well-documented, standard-library-only client for the public Open Targets Platform GraphQL API. Script behaviour (identifier resolution, target/disease/drug records, association and evidence paging) matches the manifest description and the bundled reference files, which contain only schema documentation and GraphQL examples with no embedded instructions directed at the agent. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt-injection, concealment, or role-redefinition language; its long description is a legitimate, domain-specific trigger list rather than keyword baiting. The `raw` subcommand reads a user-specified .graphql file and sends it to the API, which is explicit, user-initiated, and does not execute local code. Overall the package appears benign.

findings.title: Declared allowed-tools (Write, Edit) broader than the skill's demonstrated behaviour
findings.description: The manifest declares `allowed-tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash`, but the documented workflow only reads bundled reference files and runs read-only Python CLIs that print results to stdout; no component writes or edits files. This is an over-broad declaration rather than a violation (no code exceeds the declared permissions), so it is informational only.

findings.title: GraphQL endpoint is overridable via environment variable and CLI flag
findings.description: The shared transport reads the API endpoint from the OPEN_TARGETS_API_URL environment variable and also exposes an `--api-url` override on every subcommand. If an attacker (or a poisoned environment/agent context) sets this variable, all query payloads and identifiers would be POSTed to an arbitrary host instead of api.platform.opentargets.org. The transmitted data is low-sensitivity (public gene/disease/drug identifiers and GraphQL documents), and configurable endpoints are a common, legitimate pattern, so impact is limited.
findings.remediation: Optionally validate that the configured endpoint uses HTTPS and warn on stderr when a non-default host is used, so redirection of traffic is visible to the user.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The openfda skill is a well-engineered, benign research tool for querying the FDA's public openFDA REST APIs. All three scripts (fda_adverse.py, fda_approvals.py, fda_labels.py) plus the shared _common.py use only the Python standard library, perform read-only HTTPS GET requests exclusively against https://api.fda.gov, and emit results to stdout/stderr as TSV/CSV/JSON. No evidence was found of: eval/exec/os.system/subprocess usage, shell invocation, file writes outside stdout, credential or environment harvesting (the only env vars read are the documented OPENFDA_API_KEY and OPENFDA_API_URL), hardcoded secrets, base64/hex obfuscation, dynamic code loading, or data exfiltration to third-party hosts. Drug/reaction arguments are passed as URL query parameters via urllib.parse.urlencode with a quote() helper that strips double quotes, so there is no injection path into a shell or interpreter; the worst case is a malformed Lucene query returning HTTP 404. Pagination logic is explicitly bounded (MAX_SKIP=25000, clamp_limit to 1000, MAX_ATTEMPTS=4 with backoff capped at 30s), so there are no unbounded loops or resource-exhaustion patterns. The SKILL.md markdown body contains no prompt injection, role redefinition, concealment directives, or safety-bypass language in any language; its imperative statements are ordinary analytical guidance, and it actively instructs honest, hedged reporting. Bundled reference files (references/api-reference.md, references/endpoint-fields.md, references/disproportionality.md) are internal to the package and contain only legitimate technical and statistical documentation. Some referenced paths under assets/ and templates/ were not found, but these appear to be scanner path-permutation artifacts of the references/ links actually used in SKILL.md and are not a security concern. The declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are broader than the skill strictly needs (it only reads bundled docs and runs Bash to invoke Python), but the code never exceeds the declared permissions, so there is no violation. Overall risk: LOW.

findings.title: Keyword-baiting trigger list in skill description

While all keywords are tightly scoped to the skill's genuine functionality (FDA public API queries) and therefore not deceptive, enumerating trigger keywords is a discovery-influencing pattern worth noting. No capability inflation or brand impersonation beyond the legitimate data source is present.
findings.snippet: Also trigger on openFDA, api.fda.gov, FAERS, Drugs@FDA, SPL, NDC, pharmacovigilance, boxed warning, adverse event report, drug recall, or safety signal.

findings.title: API endpoint overridable via environment variable and --base-url flag
findings.description: The HTTP base URL is read from the OPENFDA_API_URL environment variable and can also be overridden per-invocation with --base-url. If an attacker could set that environment variable or inject the flag, all queries (including the optional OPENFDA_API_KEY which _build_url appends as a query parameter) would be redirected to an attacker-controlled host, leaking the API key and returning attacker-controlled data to the agent. findings.title: Medical/pharmacovigilance output requires careful interpretation

Notably, the skill itself mitigates this extensively: SKILL.md and references/disproportionality.md repeatedly state that FAERS counts reports rather than patients, list six reasons a signal is not a risk, mandate quoting 'a' alongside every ratio, and require the phrasing "reports mention this event disproportionately" instead of causal language. The single Python script uses argparse, pandas and standard library only: it reads a local CSV path supplied via the PRIMEKG_DATA environment variable or --data flag, performs substring and equality filtering on DataFrame columns, and prints TSV/JSON to stdout. findings.title: Unbounded in-memory load of a multi-gigabyte CSV
findings.description: _load_kg() reads the entire ~4M-row PrimeKG edge list into a pandas DataFrame and caches it in a module-level dictionary, consuming several GB of RAM. The two-hop path search additionally performs nested per-row iteration over frontier edges, which can be expensive for hub nodes with very large degree. This is documented in the compatibility field and is inherent to the stated purpose, so it is an operational/resource consideration rather than a deliberate DoS, but it can exhaust memory or CPU on constrained hosts.

findings.remediation: Consider chunked reading or column pruning (usecols) and cap the number of returned two-hop paths / intermediate nodes to bound memory and CPU usage.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: This is a legitimate, well-constructed scientific computing skill for de novo protein binder design. All three bundled Python scripts are standard-library-only and perform read-only, offline computation: binder_target_spec.py parses a local PDB and computes geometric neighbour counts; binder_filter.py reads a metrics CSV and applies numeric thresholds; design_manifest.py does arithmetic on campaign cost. There are no network calls (no requests, urllib, socket, curl), no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no file writes, no environment-variable or credential access, no base64/hex obfuscation, and no hardcoded secrets. File access is strictly limited to user-specified --pdb/--csv paths and stdin; there is no directory traversal or over-collection. The SKILL.md body contains no prompt-injection, role-redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language — in fact it emphasises honest reporting of limitations. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are a superset of what the scripts actually do (the scripts themselves never write files), so there is no tool-restriction violation. The referenced documentation files are bundled internally and contain only domain guidance. Findings are limited to minor hygiene issues: a trigger-keyword list in the description, documentation of an unpinned upstream git clone + install script, and an O(n^2) distance loop. Note on dual-use: the skill concerns protein binder design, a legitimate and widely published open-science domain (BindCraft/RFdiffusion are public, MIT-licensed, Nature-published tools), and the content provides no uplift toward harmful biological agents — it focuses on target selection, metric interpretation, and honest reporting of failure rates.

findings.title: O(n^2) pairwise distance computation over PDB residues
findings.description: neighbour_counts() performs an all-pairs distance calculation over every parsed residue with no upper bound on input size. A very large user-supplied PDB (e.g., a large assembly with tens of thousands of residues) would cause quadratic CPU growth. This is a local, bounded-by-input-file performance characteristic typical of simple structural tooling rather than a deliberate DoS, and the script is read-only with no network or recursion.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The pytdc skill is a well-scoped, defensively engineered scientific tooling package. findings.title: Remote dataset and model-checkpoint downloads (pickled artifacts) from third-party hosts

Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with running local Python scripts, and the declared compatibility note accurately discloses the outbound network access the scripts perform. Only minor, low-severity hygiene issues were identified: an explicit trigger-keyword list in the description, environment/CLI-overridable API base URLs without host allowlisting, and generous network timeouts with retry backoff.

findings.title: API endpoints overridable via environment variables and CLI flags
findings.description: Both API base URLs are read from the environment (GNOMAD_API_URL, GWAS_API_URL) and can also be overridden with --gnomad-url / --gwas-url. A poisoned environment or a crafted command line could point the clients at an attacker-controlled host, sending gene-symbol queries there and returning attacker-controlled JSON that is then summarised by the agent. Impact is low because no credentials, local file contents, or secrets are transmitted (only gene symbols) and no response content is executed, but it is an unvalidated network destination.

Invoking the scripts with many gene symbols or a large --limit against a slow endpoint could consume substantial wall-clock time. Mitigations are present (per-gene --limit defaults of 100-200, MAX_PAGE_SIZE cap, bounded retries), so this is informational rather than a true DoS primitive.

TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 120
MAX_ATTEMPTS = 4
BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS = 2.0
findings.remediation: Add an overall wall-clock budget across the symbol loop and document expected runtime for multi-gene invocations.

findings.title: Service-supplied URLs and filenames used for local file writes
findings.description: fetch_structure.py downloads files whose URLs come from the AlphaFold API response body (cifUrl, pdbUrl, paeDocUrl) and derives the output filename with Path(url).name. If the upstream service were compromised or spoofed (e.g., DNS/MITM), the URL could point off-domain and the written filename is partly attacker-influenced. Risk is low: the request layer is HTTPS-only to well-known public endpoints, Path(url).name strips directory components (preventing traversal), downloads are size-capped at 256 MB, and files are written only under the user-specified --out-dir. Content is never executed or interpreted as instructions.
findings.snippet:
wanted = {"cif": prediction.get("cifUrl"), "pdb": prediction.get("pdbUrl"), ...}
...
destination = out_dir / Path(url).name
size = download(url, destination)
findings.remediation: Validate that service-returned URLs match an allow-list of expected hosts (alphafold.ebi.ac.uk) and sanitize the derived filename against an expected pattern before writing to disk.
